newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock dive seen spilling into foreign marts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock dive seen spilling into foreign marts.

text.p: Jittery investors bailed out of the U.S. stock market Thursday amid new signs short term interest rates may soon rise, and traders predicted Wall Street's new nervousness will impact foreign markets.

"It will probably spill over to the rest of the world," said a trader at a large Asian bank in New York, who did not want to be idenitified. "The bond market is nervous because of interest rates and the currency market is bid up on the perception that higher rates will boost the dollar, athough that is not necessarily true."

The Dow industrials fell 160 points to 6879, a big drop in point terms and wider than usual, but not an extraordinary decline measured by percent. The Dow, which was down 2.28 percent, closed near its low for the day. Only Tuesday, the Dow had set an all-time closing high of 7085.

Long-term interest rates approached seven percent Thursday with the long Treasury bond down nearly a point. The dollar rose above 1.70 marks and 123 yen by lunch time in New York, closing at 123.40/45 yen and 1.7050/60 marks. Fresh economic data early in the day got the markets off to a rocky start.
U.S. retail sales rose a larger-than-expected 0.8 percent in February, while first-time weekly jobless claims rose 307,000, a smaller increase than forecast.

"I do expect a negative effect on foreign markets, but I do not expect it to be substantial," said Rao Chalasani, market strategist at EVEREN Securities. He noted that foreign markets, which have been hitting new highs too, were weak Thursday before the U.S. open.
Chalasani said the U.S. bond market will be a key determinant for stocks. U.S. stocks could fall "a few hundred points if the bonds go over seven percent," he said.

Unlike some analysts, Chalasani does not expect an increase in short rates when the Federal Reserve's policy- setting group meets on March 25. For one thing, the markets are doing just what the Federal Reserve seems to want, judging by chairman Alan Greenspan's concerns about irrational exuberance voiced at the end of 1996, he said.

On Thursday, Michael Moskow, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, said the Fed is monitoring U.S. financial markets as it gets ready for the policy meeting. He added that he expects 2.0-2.5 percent economic growth in 1997 and a pickup in inflation to 3.0 percent.
Marion Schultheis, senior vice president and senior portfolio manager at IDS Advisory Group said the Fed could raise short rates 25 basis points, but "after today that's in the market."
She said a big concern seems to be wage inflation, but added: "That's a little bit of a scare that's not warranted."

She said the stock market has been setting records because inflation has been subdued and corporate profits have been doing well. If short rates do rise later in the month, that could reassure investors that the Fed is determined to keep inflation in check, she said.
William LeFevre of Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum, agreed that the market is factoring in a tightening by the Fed.
"The statistics this morning suggested the economy is much stronger than earlier thought," he said. "The long bond yield is nearing seven percent and that's where they jump out the window."
Eric Miller, strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said a Fed tigthening was a minority view as recently as a few days ago, but that is changing in the face of a string of data.
The immediate effect is that money managers "will have difficulty getting bold" so "a period of uncertainty is likely to persist" until March 25.
